title: The Vacuum and the Key Exchange: Hellman, the Fifty-Six Bits, and the Second Career in Risk
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: New York City, the birth
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the place pin is a reconstruction, since the sources give only New York City for the birth and locate the Bronx solely as where he grows up
stops.campa: Martin Edward Hellman is born on the second of October, 1945, to a Jewish family in New York City. The war has been over seven weeks. The sources that record the birth name the city and no borough; the Bronx enters the record later, as the place he grows up, and he keeps returning to it in interviews as the measure of every later comfort. He calls the household relatively poor by the standards of the Peninsula he will spend his life on, tight rather than destitute. The borough teaches him no mathematics. It teaches him how to get by without complaining.
suggested_refs: Computer History Museum oral history X6076.2011, in which Hellman locates his childhood in the Bronx
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011, 11 March 2011

stops.name: Bronx High School of Science, the competitive exam
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; only the 1963 diploma is attested, and the entry year is inferred from a four-year course
stops.campa: The Bronx High School of Science has occupied its building on West 205th Street since the third of March, 1959, and it selects its entrants by competitive examination. Hellman takes the exam, passes it, and leaves with a diploma in 1963. No interview names a teacher, a classroom, a rivalry, or a single afternoon out of these four years. The record states the school and the year and then stops, and this journey stops there too, because the school's statistical reputation for producing engineers is not evidence about this particular boy.
suggested_refs: The 205th Street building of the Bronx High School of Science, occupied from 3 March 1959

stops.name: University Heights, the engineering degree
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed from ordinary commencement practice
stops.campa: New York University's College of Engineering does not sit at Washington Square. It sits on the University Heights campus in the Bronx, where it has been since 1894 and where it stays until NYU sells the site in 1973. Hellman earns a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering there in 1966, a short ride from the high school: circuits, systems, and no cryptography whatever. The curriculum points him at nothing he will later be known for. He crosses the continent the same year, and the Bronx stops being an address and becomes a reference point.
suggested_refs: The NYU University Heights campus, sold in 1973 and now Bronx Community College

stops.name: Stanford, the master's degree
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed
stops.campa: Hellman arrives at Stanford for graduate work and takes a master's in electrical engineering in 1967. The campus he steps onto now will hold him as a student, then as a professor for twenty-five years, then as an emeritus, and finally simply as a resident: he ends up living on its grounds. Thomas M. Cover takes him on as a doctoral student. Information theory is the discipline, and it is the reason cryptography will later look to him like a field he already owns rather than a field he is trespassing in.
suggested_refs: Thomas M. Cover's information theory group at Stanford, 1966 to 1969

stops.name: Yorktown Heights, lunch with Horst Feistel
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed. Pin inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json
stops.campa: In the Saarinen building at Yorktown Heights, Hellman spends a year at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center. Horst Feistel is in the same department, running the cryptographic effort that will become the Data Encryption Standard, and the two of them take lunch together regularly. Feistel explains how ciphers work. Hellman watches a corporation spend real money on secrecy and reads it as a forecast: commerce is going to need this. He names it later as one of three events that turn him toward the field. The other two are still ahead of him.
suggested_refs: The Eero Saarinen building at Kitchawan Road, Yorktown Heights, where Feistel's cipher work began
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011, 11 March 2011

stops.name: Stanford, Learning with Finite Memory
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed
stops.campa: The dissertation is called Learning with Finite Memory, and Thomas Cover signs it in 1969. Its problem is how much a machine can infer when it cannot remember everything it has seen, a question about the economy of information rather than about codes. Hellman leaves Stanford holding a doctorate in exactly the discipline that Claude Shannon had already shown, twenty years earlier, to contain cryptography whole. Nobody has told him this yet. The man who tells him is waiting in Cambridge, three thousand miles east.
suggested_refs: Hellman's 1969 Stanford dissertation, Learning with Finite Memory

stops.name: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the Shannon paper from Peter Elias
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed from the academic calendar. Pin inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json
stops.campa: Hellman teaches two years at MIT as an assistant professor of electrical engineering. Peter Elias, one of the founders of information theory, hands him a paper by Claude Shannon, and the paper makes plain that cryptography is a branch of the field Hellman took his doctorate in. That is the third spark and it is the one that catches. He leaves Cambridge in 1971 already reading the subject as his own property, and colleagues at three institutions keep telling him that working on it is professional suicide.
suggested_refs: Claude Shannon, 'Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems', Bell System Technical Journal, 1949
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011, 11 March 2011

segments.name: The Vacuum, and the Laboratory of Three

stops.name: Stanford, the assistant professorship and the warnings
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed from the academic calendar
stops.campa: Hellman joins the Stanford electrical engineering faculty as an assistant professor and begins a run of twenty-five years. The advice he receives is uniform: the National Security Agency already knows anything he could discover, and would classify it if he found something new. He works several years in what he calls a vacuum. Nobody funds the work and colleagues press him to drop it. Whitfield Diffie has been five miles away since November 1969, at the Artificial Intelligence Laboratory on the hill above Felt Lake. The two men do not meet for another five years.
suggested_refs: The Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory above Felt Lake, Diffie's address from November 1969
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011

stops.name: Yorktown Heights, Konheim gives Diffie a name
stops.date_confidence: attested to summer 1974; day reconstructed. Pin inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json
stops.campa: Whitfield Diffie, two years into unfunded private research, tours the Watson Research Center with Mary Fischer and meets Feistel's group. Alan Konheim, the group's director, cannot share the classified work. He gives Diffie the one unclassified thing he has, which is a name and a place. Six years after Hellman ate lunch in this building, the building sends him a collaborator. Konheim barely knows either man. The name is the whole of what he gives, and he gives it because the classified material in the next room is the one thing he cannot.
stops.quote: a professor at Stanford working the same problem... Martin Hellman
stops.quote_source: Alan Konheim to Whitfield Diffie, Yorktown Heights, summer 1974, as recorded in diffie.journey.json
suggested_refs: Alan Konheim's referral, the only unclassified thing IBM could hand over
sources: diffie.journey.json, stop 'Yorktown Heights: the Watson Research Center, and a name'

stops.name: Stanford, the half hour that runs to eleven at night
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1974 in the atlas file; the day is a default
stops.campa: Diffie telephones Stanford and is granted half an hour. The meeting runs to eleven at night and Diffie stays for dinner. Hellman calls it afterward a meeting of the minds, and what he means is narrower and stranger than affection: it is the first time in years that anyone has failed to tell him he is wasting his career. He hires Diffie the following spring as a part-time research programmer. It is the end of a two-year stretch of unfunded, unwelcome research for both men, a road trip that had no destination until this evening produced one.
suggested_refs: Hellman's office in the Stanford electrical engineering department, autumn 1974
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011
diffie.journey.json, stop 'Stanford, the half hour that runs into the evening'

stops.name: Berkeley, the third fool
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the sources give a range of 1974 to 1975 and no month
stops.campa: Ralph Merkle, a student across the bay at Berkeley, has reached the key distribution problem on his own and from a different direction. A mutual friend, overhearing Diffie and Merkle circle the same difficulty, suggests the three of them meet. Hellman describes Merkle as another fool crazy enough to work in the area. In 1974 that is the highest compliment available in the discipline, because the discipline, in the open literature of the United States, consists of approximately these three men and no others.
suggested_refs: Merkle's Berkeley project on secure communication over insecure channels, developed independently
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011

stops.name: Stanford, Merkle brought across the bay
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; June 1975 is the atlas date for Diffie's enrolment and Merkle's arrival is placed with it
stops.campa: Merkle finishes his master's at Berkeley and Hellman, in his own verb, kidnaps him: brings him to Stanford for a doctorate under a nominal supervision that Hellman insists was never really supervision. Diffie enrols the same June as a doctoral student under Hellman's sponsorship, and never takes the degree, an unsatisfied physical examination standing in the way. For the first time the three of them are in one place, holding three adjacent pieces of one idea, and not one of the pieces is yet a published paper.
suggested_refs: The Stanford cryptography group of 1975: Hellman, Diffie, Merkle
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011
diffie.journey.json, stop 'Stanford, the doctorate not taken'

stops.name: Stanford, the DES review recorded on tape
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1976; month and day are defaults. One source stretches the episode across 1975 to 1976 and another dates the published critique to June 1977; the contradiction is left standing
stops.campa: Diffie and Hellman convene a review of the proposed Data Encryption Standard at Stanford, with Dennis Branstad of the National Bureau of Standards and representatives of the National Security Agency in the room. Their argument is arithmetic: fifty-six bits is a key space that a well-funded adversary can simply walk through. The session is recorded on audio. Declassified agency history later states plainly what the room was circling, which is that the key had been argued down from sixty-four and then settled by compromise.
stops.quote: tried to convince IBM to reduce the length of the key from 64 to 48 bits. Ultimately they compromised on a 56-bit key.
stops.quote_source: Declassified NSA history, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Data Encryption Standard'
suggested_refs: The audio recording of the 1976 Stanford DES review

stops.name: Gaithersburg, the National Bureau of Standards
stops.date_confidence: the workshops are attested to the 1975 to 1977 dispute; no date for a Hellman visit exists, because no visit is attested
stops.campa: The National Bureau of Standards, which proposed the standard, holds two open workshops nationally to air the dispute over key length. Gaithersburg is the agency's address and the institutional counterparty to everything Hellman argues in these years. Whether he ever stands in the building is recorded in no source reached for this journey: the workshops are attested, his physical presence at them is not. The pin marks the adversary's office rather than a visit, and the journey declines to invent the visit.
suggested_refs: The two NBS open workshops on the Data Encryption Standard

stops.name: New York, the editor's invitation
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the invitation is attested only in oral history, with no date, and is placed here ahead of the November issue
stops.campa: Jim Massey, editor of the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, invites Hellman to write up the cryptography work, and agrees to make it a joint paper once Diffie is drawn in. The invitation is the ordinary machinery of a learned society, and it is the machinery by which a subject the government considers its own passes into open print. Merkle's parallel result goes elsewhere, to Communications of the ACM, submitted independently and earlier, and it appears in April 1978, a year and a half behind the paper it anticipates.
suggested_refs: IEEE headquarters at 345 East 47th Street, New York, in 1976
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011

stops.name: Stanford, New Directions in Cryptography
stops.date_confidence: issue month attested; day is a default
stops.campa: The paper appears in the November 1976 issue of the IEEE Transactions on Information Theory. It defines public key cryptosystems, digital signatures, and the exchange that will carry both authors' names, and it builds the last of these out of modular exponentiation, the arithmetic Carl Friedrich Gauss set down in the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae in 1801. The mathematics waits a hundred and seventy-five years in the open, unclassified and unused, published and public the entire time, for somebody with a reason to want it.
stops.quote: We stand today on the brink of a revolution in cryptography.
stops.quote_source: Whitfield Diffie and Martin E. Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory IT-22, no. 6 (November 1976), p. 644, opening sentence
suggested_refs: 'New Directions in Cryptography', IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, November 1976

stops.name: Stanford, the sentence that is not mathematics
stops.date_confidence: the date is the atlas convention for the closing paragraph of the November 1976 paper, not a separate event
stops.campa: The paper closes with a sentence no referee could check. It is a recruitment notice and a political claim at once, written jointly and on purpose. The popular version has the government monopoly breaking at that instant, which overstates the case: the monopoly does not break, it is put on notice and then contested for twenty years. What the sentence accomplishes immediately is to bring the agency's attention onto two men who have not yet been threatened with anything.
stops.quote: We hope this will inspire others...in which participation has been discouraged...by a nearly total government monopoly
stops.quote_source: Diffie and Hellman, 'New Directions in Cryptography', closing paragraph, as elided in diffie.journey.json, stop 'Stanford, the sentence that is not mathematics'
suggested_refs: The closing paragraph of the 1976 paper, quoted more often than the mathematics
sources: diffie.journey.json, stop 'Stanford, the sentence that is not mathematics'

segments.name: The Prosecution That Does Not Happen

stops.name: Fort George G. Meade, the letter from Joseph A. Meyer
stops.date_confidence: attested to July 1977; day is a default. The pin is the agency's headquarters, not Meyer's home address, which no reachable source locates. Pin inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json
stops.campa: An employee of the National Security Agency named Joseph A. Meyer writes to the IEEE from his home address in Maryland, warning that publishing and exporting cryptography papers can carry five to ten years in prison and heavy fines. It is not an official communication of the agency and it is not signed on the agency's behalf. It does not need to be. The letter moves the question of criminal prosecution off the corridor and onto the desk of Stanford's general counsel, where it acquires a file.
suggested_refs: The Meyer letter of July 1977 to the IEEE
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011

stops.name: Stanford, the general counsel's opinion
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the meeting falls between the July 1977 letter and the October 1977 symposium, with no date given in the oral history
stops.campa: Hellman carries the letter to John Schwartz, Stanford's general counsel. Schwartz reads it and gives an opinion: if the export control statute is drawn wide enough to cover the papers, then the statute is unconstitutional. He adds that this is an opinion and not a guarantee. The university will defend Hellman through appeal. The university cannot pay his fine or serve his sentence once he is legally a criminal. Hellman describes the conversation afterward as reassuring, which is an odd word for it, and he uses it anyway.
suggested_refs: The general counsel's opinion on export control and the First Amendment, Stanford, 1977
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011

stops.name: Cornell University, the two papers read for the students
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1977; day is a default
stops.campa: At the IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory at Cornell, Hellman reads two joint papers that his students wrote with him, one with Ralph Merkle and one with Stephen Pohlig. Schwartz had advised that a tenured professor survives a multiyear prosecution and a graduate student does not; the students' parents, hearing this, prevail on their sons to stand down. Hellman places each student at the podium beside him while he speaks, so that nobody in the room can mistake the authorship. No prosecution follows.
suggested_refs: The 1977 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory at Cornell
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011

stops.name: Fort George G. Meade, Inman and the voluntary review
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the sources date the Inman exchanges only to the late 1970s. Pin inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json
stops.campa: Admiral Bobby Inman, director of the National Security Agency, is trying to have Congress declare cryptographic research born classified, whether or not the researcher has ever touched classified material. Against his own agency's advice, he and Hellman come to know each other directly. Hellman's argument is practical rather than constitutional: the policy would alienate the very authors the agency needs cooperating. Inman converts the review process from mandatory to voluntary. Diffie had been turned away at this fence in 1973.
suggested_refs: The voluntary prepublication review arrangement for cryptographic papers
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011

segments.name: The Patent, the Knapsack, and the Dispersal

stops.name: Washington, D.C., the patent filed and the patent granted
stops.date_confidence: filing date attested exactly; the grant of 29 April 1980 is attested separately. Pin is the atlas canonical Washington station, inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json
stops.campa: United States Patent 4,200,770, Cryptographic Apparatus and Method, is filed on the sixth of September, 1977, assigned to the Leland Stanford Junior University, naming Diffie, Hellman, and Merkle as inventors. It is granted on the twenty-ninth of April, 1980. The loose date in circulation is 1977, which is the filing and not the grant, and two and a half years of examination separate them. The patent long since expired, outlasted by an internet that runs the exchange it once claimed to own on nearly every connection made. Washington, on this occasion, is simply where the paperwork was filed and processed.
suggested_refs: US Patent 4,200,770, filed 6 September 1977, granted 29 April 1980

stops.name: Stanford, the knapsack
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are defaults
stops.campa: Hellman and Merkle publish the knapsack cryptosystem, an early candidate for public key encryption built on the subset sum problem rather than on discrete logarithms. It is a second route to the same destination, and it is a route that closes: Adi Shamir breaks the basic scheme in 1982, four years after publication. The founding paper had described a shape for a cipher and invited anyone at all to fill it. Shamir's break is one of the things the invitation brings back.
suggested_refs: The Merkle-Hellman knapsack cryptosystem, published 1978, broken by Shamir in 1982

stops.name: San Jose, the collaborators disperse
stops.date_confidence: 1980 per the Merkle biography; the oral history places the move at 1979, and the contradiction is not resolved here
stops.campa: Merkle takes his Stanford doctorate in 1979 and goes to Elxsi in San Jose as manager of compiler development, moving to Xerox PARC in 1988 and later into nanotechnology. Diffie has already gone to Northern Telecom in Mountain View, where he runs secure systems research from 1978 to 1991. Hellman stays where he is. The laboratory of two that became a laboratory of three lasted about four years and produced one paper and one patent. It then dissolved into three ordinary careers on three separate payrolls.
suggested_refs: Elxsi Corporation, San Jose, Merkle's first employer after Stanford
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011

stops.name: Redwood City, the royalty dispute
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the oral history dates the dispute only to the 1980s
stops.campa: RSA Data Security forms around the rival algorithm, and the founding RSA paper credits Diffie, Hellman, and Merkle with inventing public key cryptography. When Stanford asks to be paid, the company's position becomes that the Stanford patents are invalid. Hellman is angry for some years about it. He comes round later to crediting Jim Bidzos with building the industry that eventually makes the invention worth something to its inventors as well. The credit in the paper and the position in the negotiation are both sincere.
suggested_refs: The RSA Data Security dispute over the validity of the Stanford public key patents
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011

stops.name: Palo Alto, Beyond War
stops.date_confidence: the movement's establishment is dated to 1984; one account of Hellman's involvement gives 1985 and another 1982, and the three dates are left standing
stops.campa: Beyond War is established in the Palo Alto area, drawing on the university, the computer industry, and the marketing trade, and arguing that human thinking about conflict has to change to match the destructive power the species now holds. Hellman's own biography places him among its founders and names him principal editor of the movement's booklet, Beyond War: A New Way of Thinking. The independent account of the movement credits Richard T. Roney as that booklet's editor and does not mention Hellman anywhere.
suggested_refs: Beyond War: A New Way of Thinking, the movement's founding booklet

stops.name: San Francisco, the spacebridge to Moscow
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are defaults. Hellman's presence in the San Francisco hall is not attested
stops.campa: Beyond War gives its annual award to International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War over a live satellite link joining Moscow and San Francisco, watched by more than seventy-five thousand people. The movement stages its most visible act directly across the fault line it exists to argue about. Hellman is inside the organization at this point by his own account. Whether he is in the San Francisco hall on the night is recorded in no source reached here, and the pin marks the event rather than the man.
suggested_refs: The 1984 Moscow to San Francisco satellite spacebridge staged by Beyond War

stops.name: Stanford, the Nazi within
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the op-ed is undated on Hellman's page and is placed at the Bitburg visit of May 1985, which its filename and subject indicate
stops.campa: Hellman publishes an op-ed occasioned by the Bitburg cemetery visit, asking how either superpower can condemn the Nazis while thirty thousand American and twenty thousand Soviet warheads stand ready. The enemy he names is not a nation. It is the psychology of war itself, the thing that lets ordinary people conduct atrocities and then go home to dinner. The cryptographer who spent a decade arguing that fifty-six bits was too few is applying the same instinct here, which is to size a bad outcome before it arrives.
stops.quote: Nuclear war is not war. It is suicide and genocide rolled into one.
suggested_refs: Hellman's op-ed 'The Nazi Within', ee.stanford.edu/~hellman/opinion/bitburg.html

stops.name: Moscow, Breakthrough with Anatoly Gromyko
stops.date_confidence: publication year attested; month and day are defaults, and the editorial work runs from about 1985
stops.campa: Hellman co-edits Breakthrough: Emerging New Thinking with Anatoly Gromyko in Moscow, more than thirty Soviet and Western scholars arguing in one volume for a shared exit from nuclear confrontation. It is published simultaneously in Russian and in English in 1987. The sponsoring committee of the Soviet Academy of Sciences is headed by Evgeni Velikhov, Gorbachev's chief science adviser. The professor who was warned that his work would be classified is now editing a book with the other side of the thing doing the classifying.
suggested_refs: Breakthrough: Emerging New Thinking, published simultaneously in Russian and English, 1987

stops.name: Washington, D.C., the committee on national cryptography policy
stops.date_confidence: committee service attested to 1994 with the report in 1996; the meeting venue is standard practice for the National Research Council and is not confirmed for this committee
stops.campa: Hellman sits on the National Research Council's Committee to Study National Cryptography Policy, whose 1996 report frames the following decade of argument over export controls on encryption software. Seventeen years after the letter from Maryland, the question of whether cryptography may be published and sold is being settled by a committee he has a seat on rather than by a prosecutor. The Academy's Washington headquarters is where committees of this kind customarily meet; this one's meeting sites are named nowhere.
suggested_refs: The 1996 National Research Council report on national cryptography policy

stops.name: Stanford, the Pioneer Award and secrecy obsolete
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; month and day are defaults. The op-ed carries no date on Hellman's page and is attached here by theme
stops.campa: The Electronic Frontier Foundation gives Hellman a Pioneer Award for the advocacy rather than for the mathematics. He has by now written the argument out plainly in an op-ed whose title is a joke at his own expense, since a cryptographer is the last person expected to say it out loud. The claim underneath concerns two goals rather than privacy. A tool built for winning a war becomes a liability to anyone trying to prevent one, and by 1994 Hellman has changed which of the two he works on.
stops.quote: Secrecy is useful if you hope to win a war, but is harmful if you are trying to prevent a war.
suggested_refs: Hellman's op-ed 'Secrecy is Obsolete', ee.stanford.edu/~hellman/opinion/secrecy.html

stops.name: Stanford, emeritus after twenty-five years
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are defaults
stops.campa: Hellman takes emeritus status as a full professor after twenty-five years on the Stanford faculty. He arrived in 1971 warned by everyone he respected that the subject was closed, occupied, and dangerous. He leaves the full-time faculty in the year the National Research Council reports to Congress on the policy question he raised, with the standard he attacked still in federal use and two years away from being broken in public. Nothing on the campus is named after him. He does not leave the campus.
suggested_refs: Hellman's Stanford emeritus appointment, 1996

stops.name: Cheltenham, the classified priority
stops.date_confidence: disclosure year attested; month and day are defaults. One source dates the classified work to 1969, another spreads it over 1969 to 1974
stops.campa: Government Communications Headquarters discloses that James Ellis, Clifford Cocks, and Malcolm Williamson had worked out the concepts of public key cryptography inside the building years before the Stanford paper, and had kept them classified. The disclosure does not settle priority so much as split it in two: the idea exists first inside the secrecy apparatus and exists usefully only once it is outside. Both of those statements are true and the sources reached here do not reconcile them.
suggested_refs: The 1997 GCHQ disclosure of the Ellis, Cocks, and Williamson work

stops.name: San Francisco, Deep Crack breaks the standard
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month reconstructed. The pin is the Electronic Frontier Foundation's city, not a confirmed site for the machine
stops.campa: The Electronic Frontier Foundation builds a purpose-made machine and uses it to break a Data Encryption Standard message in under three days. The argument Hellman and Diffie made in a recorded room at Stanford twenty-two years earlier, that fifty-six bits is a walkable space for anybody with money, is settled by demonstration instead of by debate. The standard had been federal policy the entire time. The vindication arrives as a press event, and the policy changes within three years of it.
suggested_refs: The EFF DES cracker, 'Deep Crack', 1998

stops.name: Bologna, the Marconi Prize
stops.date_confidence: award year attested; the ceremony city is a reconstruction from the Marconi Society's general practice and is not confirmed for 2000
stops.campa: Hellman and Diffie share the Marconi Prize for the invention of public key cryptography. The Marconi Society of this period frequently holds its ceremonies at Bologna, Guglielmo Marconi's birthplace, and the pin sits there for that reason and no better one. The location of the 2000 ceremony is confirmed in no source reached for this journey. The prize itself is attested. The room is a reconstruction, and this journey marks it as one rather than quietly picking a city and saying nothing.
suggested_refs: The Marconi Prize, awarded jointly to Diffie and Hellman in 2000

stops.name: Stanford, NuclearRisk.org
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the founding year is given as about 2005 and is not firmly attested in any source reached
stops.campa: Hellman builds NuclearRisk.org, which does to deterrence what an actuary does to a bridge: computes the probability of the catastrophic event and then publishes the number. He claims endorsements from a former director of the National Security Agency, a Stanford president emeritus, and two Nobel laureates; the endorsers are not individually named in the sources reached here. The method descends from the same instinct behind the 1976 argument over fifty-six bits: size a danger in numbers, publicly, before it arrives, rather than take someone's word that it has been handled.
stops.quote: Society's resistance to even minor changes in our nuclear posture demonstrates that it sees little or no risk in the nuclear status quo.
stops.quote_source: Martin Hellman, 'How Risky is Nuclear Optimism?', Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists 67, no. 2 (March 2011), pp. 47-56
suggested_refs: NuclearRisk.org, maintained by Hellman from Stanford

stops.name: Alexandria, the National Inventors Hall of Fame
stops.date_confidence: induction year attested; month and day are defaults. Pin inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json; two other coordinates for this institution circulate in the material gathered here
stops.campa: Diffie, Hellman, and Merkle are inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame, whose museum sits on the Patent and Trademark Office campus at Alexandria, having moved there from Akron in 2008. The organization's headquarters remains in Ohio, and one account of this induction has that move running the other way around. It is the third joint honor for the three of them, coming after the Marconi Prize and before the Turing Award six years later.
suggested_refs: The National Inventors Hall of Fame museum at 600 Dulany Street, Alexandria
sources: diffie.journey.json, stop 'Alexandria, Virginia: the National Inventors Hall of Fame'

stops.name: Mountain View, the Fellows interview
stops.date_confidence: attested exactly
stops.campa: Hellman sits for a Fellows interview at the Computer History Museum on the eleventh of March, 2011, and walks Jon Plutte through the strongbox analogy and the Cornell papers of 1977. He mentions that he has flown a motor glider and that he lives on the Stanford campus, and he offers both as measurements taken from a fixed origin. The origin is the borough. Sixty-five years after the birth the interview keeps returning to it, unprompted, as the thing against which the rest of the life is being compared.
stops.quote: I grew up in the Bronx, okay?
stops.quote_source: Martin Hellman, Computer History Museum oral history interview X6076.2011, Mountain View, 11 March 2011
suggested_refs: Computer History Museum oral history X6076.2011, recorded 11 March 2011
sources: Computer History Museum oral history interview, X6076.2011, 11 March 2011

stops.date_confidence: award year 2015, presented June 2016; the banquet city follows ACM's general practice and the venue is unconfirmed. Pin inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json
stops.campa: The Association for Computing Machinery gives Diffie and Hellman the 2015 A. M. Turing Award, presented in June 2016, forty years after the paper. The citation credits the invention and the promulgation both, and the promulgation was the harder half. Two rival formulations circulate as though they were the citation, one taken from the association's press release and one from a secondary summary, and neither of them is the citation. The banquet is placed in San Francisco by custom, and the room is unconfirmed.
stops.quote: for inventing and promulgating both asymmetric public-key cryptography, including its application to digital signatures, and a practical cryptographic key-exchange method
stops.quote_source: ACM A. M. Turing Award citation for 2015, as printed in Wikipedia, 'Turing Award'. ACM's own award page returned HTTP 403 and could not be checked directly

stops.name: Stanford, A New Map for Relationships
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day are defaults
stops.campa: Hellman and Dorothie Hellman publish A New Map for Relationships: Creating True Love at Home and Peace on the Planet, arguing that the failure mode of a marriage and the failure mode of a deterrence posture are one failure mode, treatable by one method. Fifty years of a single marriage is the evidence offered. It is a strange second book for a Turing laureate and it is continuous with the first: both are about what two parties can establish between them without having trusted each other in advance.
suggested_refs: A New Map for Relationships, by Martin and Dorothie Hellman, 2016

stops.name: Encina Hall, Rethinking National Security
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed; the statement page carries a 2019 copyright and no publication date. Pin inherited byte-identical from diffie.journey.json
stops.campa: At the Center for International Security and Cooperation in Encina Hall, Hellman organises a joint statement called Rethinking National Security. It carries roughly fifteen signatories, among them Bobby Inman, who had once wanted this man's research born classified, along with Leon Panetta, Richard Garwin, and Jack Matlock. Hellman is the organiser and the copyright holder and not the sole author, though its opening sentences are widely quoted as his alone. Diffie returned to this same building as a visiting scholar in 2009.
stops.quote: When World War II ended in 1945 our nation was secure from attack. Since then, we have invested trillions of dollars in an effort to improve our national security.
stops.quote_source: Opening sentences of 'Rethinking National Security', a collective statement organised and signed by Hellman with about fifteen other signatories, ee.stanford.edu/~hellman/rns/statement.html, copyright 2019. Not a first-person Hellman quotation

stops.name: Stanford, the campus residence and the absent stone
stops.date_confidence: status at the time of research, August 2026; the date is the atlas convention for a living subject
stops.campa: Hellman is alive as this journey is written, professor emeritus, living on the campus that trained him and then employed him for a quarter of a century. There is no tomb to visit, no grave, no death date. There is also no plaque: no engineering milestone, no building, no marker for the key exchange turned up in any source reached here. The monument is a protocol that runs some billions of times a day and is invisible on every one of them. The absence of a stone is set down here as an absence.
stops.quote: I live on the Stanford campus
stops.quote_source: Martin Hellman, Computer History Museum oral history interview X6076.2011, 11 March 2011
